BSD is a pretty decent OS regardless of distro, although FreeBSD can go eat some dicks and like it.

Nonetheless, BSD is not Linux.

They are also not distributions.

They are operating systems.

The Berkley Systems Distribution was the original stuff, a collection of unique tools and patches to modify System V, but since BSD 4.2 the derived BSDs have been unique codebases, distinct operating systems, and not distributions.

The D in their name is a legacy component indicating the historical nature of their systems.

When people call a BSD a distribution, they're looking at Oranges from the perspective of Apples and talking about how crisp they are.

A vast majority of tools in a BSD's userland are developed entirely in-house, OpenBSD in particular has been very active in ensuring imparity by restructuring significant parts of their code to use less common but more secure code practices.

I might add that another difference:

  • With Linux, the distribution is the kernel and GNU tools, all at various versions. Each tool is updated separately, when needs arise.
  • With BSD, the kernel and the tools are considered parts of the whole. BSD4.3 refers to a specific state of kernel and tools.

I might not have stated that exactly right, but you get the idea.

Nonetheless, BSD is not Linux.

Correct.

The article says, "Like Linux, BSD is a Unix-like operating system", but that's not entirely true. BSD can trace its lineage back to Unix. Linux cannot.

On a technicality, Linux is classed as a Unix work-alike. BSD is perhaps best described as a variant.
